claim: The superior colliculus (SC) receives input from many types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs).
source: The superior colliculus (SC) represents a major visual processing station in the mammalian brain that receives input from many types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: An unsupervised clustering algorithm identified 24 functional types of SC neurons based on their visual responses.
source: An unsupervised clustering algorithm identified 24 functional types based on their visual responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and detailed in Figure 2 with statistical analysis using Bayesian information criterion.

claim: SC functional types fall into two groups: one that responds similarly to RGCs and another with more diverse and specialized stimulus selectivity.
source: They fall into two groups: one that responds similarly to RGCs and another with more diverse and specialized stimulus selectivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the dendrogram analysis in Figure 2A showing Group 1 and Group 2.

claim: The second group of SC functional types is dominant at greater depths.
source: The second group is dominant at greater depths, consistent with a vertical progression of signal processing in the SC.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4H showing depth distribution of functional types.

claim: Cells of the same functional type tend to cluster near each other in anatomical space.
source: Cells of the same functional type tend to cluster near each other in anatomical space.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by density recovery profile analysis in Figure 4.

claim: The visual representation in the SC has lower dimensionality compared to the retina.
source: Compared to the retina, the visual representation in the SC has lower dimensionality, consistent with a sifting process along the visual pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by principal component analysis in Figure 6D.

claim: The retina has approximately 15 types of bipolar cells.
source: Processing of visual information at the cell-types level starts at the retina, where the signal is split into ∼15 types of bipolar cells (Shekhar et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The retina has approximately 63 types of amacrine cells.
source: ∼63 types of amacrine cells (Yan et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The retina has approximately 40 types of retinal ganglion cells.
source: ∼40 types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs; Roska and Meister, 2014; Sanes and Masland, 2015; Baden et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: The RGCs send processed information directly to the superior colliculus.
source: The RGCs send the processed information directly to the superior colliculus (SC), an evolutionarily conserved structure found in all vertebrates (Isa et al., 2021; Basso and May, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: In the rodent, approximately 90% of RGCs project to the superficial layer of the SC.
source: In the rodent, ∼90% of RGCs project to the superficial layer of the SC (Ellis et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Each SC neuron receives inputs from about six RGCs.
source: each SC neuron receives inputs from about six RGCs (Chandrasekaran et al., 2007)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Prior work has distinguished about five cell types in the retino-recipient superficial layer by classic criteria of cell morphology and physiology.
source: By classic criteria of cell morphology and physiology, prior work has distinguished about five cell types in the retino-recipient superficial layer (Langer and Lund, 1974; May, 2006; Gale and Murphy, 2014; Wang et al., 2010; De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: Differential expression of molecular markers has been used to describe about ten types in the superficial SC.
source: Differential expression of molecular markers has been used to describe about ten types in the superficial SC (Byun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Recent work on the primary visual cortex (V1) identified 46 types of neurons based on morphology and electrophysiology.
source: By contrast, recent work on the primary visual cortex (V1) identified 46 types of neurons based on morphology and electrophysiology (Gouwens et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The number of functionally distinct cell types in the SC has been underestimated.
source: Because the major inputs to the superficial SC are from the retina and V1, we hypothesize that the number of functionally distinct cell types in the SC has been underestimated.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on comparison with other brain regions.

claim: More than 5000 neurons were recorded from 41 image planes in 16 animals from different genetic lines.
source: We recorded more than 5000 neurons from 41 image planes in 16 animals from different genetic lines, including wild-type, Vglut2-Cre, Vgat-Cre, Tac1-Cre, Rorb-Cre, and Ntsr1-Cre mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental dataset.

claim: The recordings were limited to the posterior-medial SC that corresponds to the upper lateral visual field.
source: To maintain the integrity of the overlying cortex, one is limited to the posterior-medial SC that corresponds to the upper lateral visual field (Feinberg and Meister, 2015; Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B and C.

claim: A 'chirp' stimulus was previously employed in the classification of retinal ganglion cells.
source: the full-screen 'chirp' was previously employed in the classification of retinal ganglion cells (Baden et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Neurons in any given image plane showed robust and diverse responses to visual stimuli.
source: Neurons in any given image plane showed robust and diverse responses to these stimuli (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Locomotion barely modulates the visual responses of SC neurons.
source: Because locomotion barely modulates the visual responses of SC neurons (Savier et al., 2019), we did not consider further the effects of movements.

claim: Sparse principal component analysis was performed on the raw response traces, leading to a 50-dimensional feature vector for each neuron.
source: To classify cell types based on their functional properties, we first performed a sparse principal component analysis on the raw response traces (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Mairal et al., 2009), which led to a 50-dimensional feature vector for each neuron.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: Four designed features were added: habituation index (HI), direction selectivity index (DSI), orientation selectivity index (OSI), and motion selectivity index (MSI).
source: Then we added 4 designed features that describe different aspects of the response: a habituation index (HI) computed from repeated stimuli, a direction selectivity index (DSI), an orientation selectivity index (OSI), and a motion selectivity index (MSI, see Materials and methods).

claim: The analysis focused on 3414 neurons that responded reliably to visual stimuli (signal-to-noise ratio >0.35).
